# Python Quick Reference {#sec-python-reference}

This appendix collects the Python functions used in this script, ordered by **task** – the question you have in mind ("How do I count the missing values?") rather than the library. Each entry says what the function does, gives a short example and names where it is used first. The pandas basics are introduced step by step in *Getting Started with pandas* before Chapter 1.

Notation: `df` is a DataFrame (a table), `s` a single column (a Series), `m` a mask of truth values. `np`, `pd`, `plt` and `sns` are the usual short names for NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib and seaborn (Chapter 1).

## Plain Python used throughout

| Construct | What it does | Example | Used in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `f"{x:.2f}"` | f-string: inserts values into a text. A format code after the colon controls the display: `.2f` two decimals, `+.1f` always with sign, `.1%` as a percentage, `,` thousands separator, `8.2f` or `8s` a width of 8 characters (aligned columns) | `print(f"RMSE = {rmse:.1f} MW")` | Ch. 0 and all chapters |
| `[expr for x in values]` | list comprehension: builds a list in one line, short for a loop with `append` | `[f"T{i}" for i in range(1, 10)]` | Ch. 0, 3, 4 |
| `rows.append({...})`, `pd.DataFrame(rows)` | collect results in a loop – one dictionary per row – and turn them into a table; the keys become the column names | see *Getting Started with pandas* | Ch. 0, 1, 2, 5 |
| `for key, value in d.items():` | loop over the entries of a dictionary | `for name, m in missing.items():` | Ch. 2 |
| `" + ".join(texts)` | joins texts with a separator | `" + ".join(["a", "b"])` gives `"a + b"` | Ch. 5 |
| `{key: expr for x in values}` | dictionary comprehension: like a list comprehension, but builds a dictionary | `{s: read_sensor(z, f"{s}.txt") for s in ["TS1", "TS2"]}` | Ch. 9 |

## Missing values

| Function | What it does | Example | Used in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `df.isna()` | `True` wherever a value is missing (`NaN`, `None`, `NaT`) | `df.isna().sum()` counts missing values per column | Ch. 2 |
| `df.dropna()` | removes rows with missing values | `df.dropna()` | Ch. 11 |
| `df.fillna(value)` | replaces missing values | `X.fillna(X.median())` – median imputation | Ch. 2 |
| `na_values=[...]` in `pd.read_csv` | treats codes such as `-999` as missing while reading | `pd.read_csv(f, na_values=[-999])` | Ch. 2 |

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: `is None`, `isna()` and `==`
- `x is None` checks whether *nothing* was given, e.g. an optional argument of a function: `if fname is None:`. Use `is` only for `None` – for numbers and text always use `==`.
- `s.isna()` checks whether *measured values* are missing. Never test with `== np.nan`: `NaN` is by definition not equal to anything, not even to itself – `np.nan == np.nan` is `False`.
- `s == None` on a column does not help either: it gives a mask in which even the missing values are `False`, and `if s == None:` raises an error.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## `loc` or `iloc`?
Every row has a **label** – the index shown on the left – and a **position**: first row, second row, … `loc` selects by label, `iloc` by integer position (memory aid: *i* for *integer*). As long as the index is 0, 1, 2, …, both give the same result. After sorting or filtering, they no longer do:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"T": [25, 18, 31]})   # labels 0, 1, 2
s = df.sort_values("T")                  # order now: labels 1, 0, 2
s.loc[0]     # row with the LABEL 0 → T = 25
s.iloc[0]    # FIRST row            → T = 18
```

Ranges differ, too: `df.loc[0:2]` includes the end (labels 0, 1 **and** 2), `df.iloc[0:2]` does not (positions 0 and 1, as for Python lists). For time series, including the end is convenient: `s.loc["2015-01-01":"2019-12-31"]` contains 31 December.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: `and`, `or`, `not` do not work on columns
Python's `and`, `or` and `not` handle a *single* truth value. For masks – NumPy arrays and pandas columns – use `&`, `|` and `~`, which work element by element, and put every condition in brackets:

| | single value | mask (array, column) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| and | `and` | `&` |
| or | `or` | `\|` |
| not | `not` | `~` |

```python
df[(df["machine_id"] == "M4") & (df["shift"] == "night")]   # correct
df[df["machine_id"] == "M4" & df["shift"] == "night"]       # error: & binds before ==
```

`not m` on a mask raises an error ("the truth value of an array is ambiguous"), and `~True` on a single value gives `-2`, because `~` is originally a bitwise operator on integers (newer Python versions warn about this).
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## `np.where` with one argument
With three arguments, `np.where(m, a, b)` selects values. With only one argument, `np.where(m)` does something different: it returns the *positions* where `m` is `True`. For positions, `np.flatnonzero(m)` is clearer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## `.str` and `.dt`: functions for every entry of a column
Text functions such as `strip()` work on a *single* text. To apply them to every entry of a column, pandas offers the accessor `.str`: `s.str.strip()`, `s.str.lower()`, `s.str.startswith("produkt")`. The column must contain text – hence `s.astype(str).str.strip()`. In the same way, `.dt` gives access to the parts of time stamps: `s.dt.hour`, `s.dt.day_name()`. For a time *index*, these are available directly: `df.index.hour`, `df.index.dayofweek`.

Pitfall: some functions exist twice with different meanings.

```python
s = pd.Series(["1,5", "2,0"])
s.replace(",", ".")        # replaces entries that are exactly "," – here: no change
s.str.replace(",", ".")    # replaces "," inside every text – "1.5", "2.0"
```

Forgetting `.str` raises no error – the data simply remain unchanged.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Format codes for time stamps
In `pd.to_datetime(s, format=...)`, every code stands for one complete field of the date. `%Y` always has four digits; the two-digit codes also accept a single digit when reading, so `%d/%m/%Y` reads `19/07/2008` as well as `1/8/2008`:

| Code | Meaning | Digits | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `%Y` | year | 4 | `2025` |
| `%y` | year without century | 2 | `25` |
| `%m` | month | 2 | `04` |
| `%d` | day | 2 | `11` |
| `%H` | hour (00–23) | 2 | `13` |
| `%M` | minute | 2 | `05` |
| `%S` | second | 2 | `00` |

All other characters (`-`, `.`, `:`, blanks) must appear in the format exactly as in the data. Upper and lower case matter: `%m` is the month, `%M` the minute – a classic error that often raises no error message. Other tools write formats with letters instead, e.g. `yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm` in Excel or `YYYYMMDDHH24` in the DWD documentation; such formats have to be translated.

Formats you will meet in practice:

| Data look like | Typical source | Reading in pandas |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `2025-04-11 13:00:00`, `2025-04-11T13:00:00+02:00` | international standard ISO 8601: databases, web services, modern loggers | `pd.to_datetime(s, format="ISO8601")` |
| `11.04.2025 13:00` | German software, Excel exports | `format="%d.%m.%Y %H:%M"` |
| `2025041113` | compact formats of older systems, e.g. the DWD | `format="%Y%m%d%H"` (text, not number) |
| `1744376400` | seconds since 1 January 1970 (Unix time): sensors, IoT, log files | `pd.to_datetime(s, unit="s")` |
:::

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| `.agg([...])` | several summaries at once | `.agg(["min", "mean", "max"])` | Ch. 2 |
| `s.resample("D")` | groups a time series into consecutive intervals (`"h"` hour, `"D"` day, …); needs time stamps as index | `s.resample("D").mean()` | Ch. 2 |
| `s.rolling("1D")` | window that slides along the time axis (`"1D"` = one day; `rolling(144)` = 144 values), followed by a summary such as `.mean()` | `s.rolling("1D").mean()` – 24 h rolling mean | Ch. 2 |
| `s.shift(k)` | the series shifted by `k` steps, e.g. the value of the day before | `daily.shift(7)` – the same weekday one week earlier | Ch. 11 |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Method chaining – and why pandas makes it possible
In `energy.set_index("date").sort_index()`, the second method is applied directly to the result of the first. This works because of three design decisions in pandas:

1. **Methods return a new object and leave the original unchanged.** `df.sort_values("a")` returns a sorted copy; `df` stays as it is. Plain Python does the opposite for lists: `values.sort()` sorts the list itself and returns `None` – so `values.sort().reverse()` fails, while `df.sort_values("a").head()` works.
2. **The type stays the same.** A table becomes a table, a column a column – so the next method always fits. `.str` and `.dt` also return a column.
3. **Methods instead of statements.** An assignment such as `df["temp_K"] = df["temp_C"] + 273.15` cannot be chained; `df.assign(temp_K=df["temp_C"] + 273.15)` returns a new table with the additional column. For the same reason, avoid the older option `inplace=True`: it changes the table itself and returns `None`, which breaks the chain.

Returning new tables might sound expensive. Since pandas 3.0 ("copy-on-write"), however, data are only copied when they are actually changed.

Many NumPy functions also exist as pandas methods – `s.abs()`, `s.median()`, `s.std()`. For pandas data, prefer the methods: they fit into a chain, and they skip missing values, which NumPy functions do not:

```python
s = pd.Series([1, -4, np.nan, 3])
s.abs().median()            # 3.0 – pandas skips the missing value
np.median(np.abs(s))        # nan – one missing value makes the result missing
```

The standard deviation differs, too: `s.std()` divides by $n-1$ (sample standard deviation, Chapter 2), `np.std(...)` by $n$ unless you write `ddof=1`.

For longer chains, put the whole expression in brackets – inside brackets, Python continues on the next line – and write one step per line:

```python
daily = (weather
         .dropna()            # remove rows with missing values
         .resample("D")       # group by day
         .mean())             # one mean per day
```

Chains are compact; separate steps are easier to check. A good habit: build a chain step by step, and if it fails, remove the last steps until it works again – this shows which step causes the error.
:::

## Probability distributions

SciPy offers every distribution as an object in `scipy.stats` – e.g. `stats.norm`, `stats.lognorm`, `stats.weibull_min`, `stats.t` – and all of them have the same methods. Parameters are passed as shape(s), `loc` and `scale` (Chapter 3).

| Function | What it does | Example | Used in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `dist.fit(x)` | estimates the parameters by maximum likelihood; `floc=0` fixes the location at 0 | `beta, loc, eta = stats.weibull_min.fit(x, floc=0)` | Ch. 3 |
| `dist.pdf(x, ...)`, `dist.cdf(x, ...)` | density and distribution function at `x` | `stats.weibull_min.pdf(t, beta, scale=eta)` | Ch. 3 |
| `dist.ppf(q, ...)` | quantile: the value below which a share `q` lies – the inverse of `cdf` | `stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=9)` | Ch. 3 |
| `dist.logpdf(x, ...)` | logarithm of the density; summed over the data, the log-likelihood | `stats.norm.logpdf(x, mu, sigma).sum()` | Ch. 3 |
| `dist.interval(0.95, ...)` | central interval that contains the given share | `stats.t.interval(0.95, df=n - 1, loc=x_bar, scale=se)` | Ch. 3 |

| `LinearRegression().fit(X, y)` | linear regression for prediction (module `sklearn.linear_model`); `.predict(X_new)`, coefficients in `.coef_` and `.intercept_` | `LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train).predict(X_test)` | Ch. 6 |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Three ways to fit a straight line
The script fits the same linear model with three tools – the purpose decides which one fits (see @sec-inference-prediction):

| Tool | Returns | Use it when … | Used in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `np.polyfit(x, y, deg=1)` | slope and intercept only | you need a quick line with *one* input | Ch. 1, 2 |
| `smf.ols("y ~ x1 + x2", data=df).fit()` | regression table with standard errors, confidence intervals, p-values | you want to *interpret* the model (inference) | Ch. 5 |
| `LinearRegression()` (scikit-learn) | predictions; fits into pipelines and cross-validation | you want to *predict* and check the result on new data | Ch. 6 |

scikit-learn computes the same coefficients as statsmodels, but no standard errors, confidence intervals or p-values – for inference, use statsmodels.
:::

## Machine learning with scikit-learn

All models and preprocessing steps in scikit-learn share one interface: `fit(X, y)` learns from the training data, `predict(X_new)` predicts; classifiers also offer `predict_proba(X_new)`. Preprocessing steps have `fit` and `transform`, or `fit_transform` for both at once. Imports: the module is named in the first column, e.g. `from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline`.

### Validation and model selection

| Function | What it does | Example | Used in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `make_pipeline(step1, ..., model)` (`sklearn.pipeline`) | chains preprocessing and model into one object; `fit` fits all steps on the training data only, so nothing leaks from the test data. `pipe[0]` is the first step, `pipe[-1]` the model | `make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))` | Ch. 6 |
| `train_test_split(X, y, test_size=..., stratify=y, random_state=0)` (`sklearn.model_selection`) | random split into training and test data; `stratify=y` keeps the class shares equal in both parts | `X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0)` | Ch. 7 |
| `KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)`, `StratifiedKFold(...)` (`sklearn.model_selection`) | the folds for cross-validation; stratified: the same class shares in every fold | `cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)` | Ch. 6, 7 |
| `cross_validate(model, X, y, cv=cv, scoring=...)`, `cross_val_score(...)` (`sklearn.model_selection`) | score of the model on each held-out fold; `cross_validate` also returns training scores with `return_train_score=True`. Errors appear as negative scores (`"neg_root_mean_squared_error"`), because scikit-learn always maximises a score | `-cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error").mean()` | Ch. 6, 7 |
| `cross_val_predict(model, X, y, cv=cv)` (`sklearn.model_selection`) | for every observation, the prediction of the fold model that did not see it | `y_hat = cross_val_predict(ridge, X, y, cv=cv)` | Ch. 6 |
| `RandomizedSearchCV(model, params, n_iter=25, cv=cv, scoring=...)` (`sklearn.model_selection`) | tunes hyperparameters: tries random combinations and evaluates each with cross-validation; results in `.best_params_`, `.best_score_`, `.best_estimator_` | see Chapter 8, Exercise 1 | Ch. 8 |
| `np.logspace(a, b, n)` | `n` values from $10^a$ to $10^b$, evenly spaced on a logarithmic scale – candidate values for a hyperparameter | `np.logspace(-4, 3, 30)` | Ch. 6 |

### Preparing the inputs

| Function | What it does | Example | Used in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `StandardScaler()` (`sklearn.preprocessing`) | standardises every column to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 (with the values of the training data) | `make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), RidgeCV())` | Ch. 6 |
| `PolynomialFeatures(degree)` (`sklearn.preprocessing`) | adds all powers and products of the inputs up to the given degree | `PolynomialFeatures(3)` | Ch. 6 |
| `SimpleImputer(strategy="median")` (`sklearn.impute`) | fills gaps with the median of the training data | `make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), StandardScaler())` | Ch. 9 |
| `VarianceThreshold(1e-8)` (`sklearn.feature_selection`) | removes (practically) constant columns | see Chapter 9 | Ch. 9 |
| `pd.get_dummies(df, columns=[...], drop_first=True)` | turns a categorical column into 0/1 columns, one per category (without the first) | `pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["Type"], drop_first=True)` | Ch. 7 |

### Models

| Function | What it does | Example | Used in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `RidgeCV(alphas=...)`, `LassoCV(cv=5)` (`sklearn.linear_model`) | regularised linear regression; the penalty $\lambda$ (`alpha`) is chosen by internal cross-validation; coefficients in `.coef_` | `RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-4, 3, 30))` | Ch. 6 |
| `GaussianProcessRegressor(kernel=..., normalize_y=True)` (`sklearn.gaussian_process`) | Gaussian process regression; `predict(X, return_std=True)` returns mean and standard deviation, the fitted hyperparameters are in `.kernel_`. Kernels from `sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels`: `ConstantKernel` ($\sigma_f^2$), `RBF` (length scale), `WhiteKernel` (noise) | `C(1.0) * RBF(10.0) + WhiteKernel(0.1)` | Ch. 6 |
| `LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)` (`sklearn.linear_model`) | logistic regression; `class_weight="balanced"` weights rare classes more | see Chapter 7 | Ch. 7 |
| `KNeighborsClassifier(k)` (`sklearn.neighbors`) | k-nearest neighbours (standardise the inputs first) | `make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(5))` | Ch. 7 |
| `DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=...)`, `plot_tree(tree)` (`sklearn.tree`) | decision tree and a drawing of its splits | `DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0)` | Ch. 7 |
| `RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300)`, `HistGradientBoostingClassifier()` (`sklearn.ensemble`) | random forest and gradient boosting; `random_state=0` makes the result reproducible | `RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0)` | Ch. 8 |
| `model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]` | predicted probability of the second class – with classes 0/1, of class 1 | `p = logreg.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]` | Ch. 7 |

### Evaluating classifiers

| Function | What it does | Example | Used in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)` (`sklearn.metrics`) | counts of all combinations of true and predicted class; for two classes, `.ravel()` gives tn, fp, fn, tp | `tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred).ravel()` | Ch. 7 |
| `ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_estimator(model, X, y)` (`sklearn.metrics`) | draws the confusion matrix; `normalize="true"` shows shares per true class | see Chapter 8 | Ch. 7, 8 |
| `classification_report(y_true, y_pred)` (`sklearn.metrics`) | precision, recall and F1 per class, with averages | `print(classification_report(y_test, model.predict(X_test)))` | Ch. 7 |
| `precision_recall_fscore_support(...)`, `recall_score(..., average=None)` (`sklearn.metrics`) | the same metrics as arrays, one value per class, for further calculations | see Chapter 8 | Ch. 8 |
| `RocCurveDisplay.from_estimator(...)`, `PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_estimator(...)` (`sklearn.metrics`) | ROC curve and precision–recall curve | `RocCurveDisplay.from_estimator(model, X_test, y_test)` | Ch. 7 |
| `roc_auc_score(y_true, score)` (`sklearn.metrics`) | area under the ROC curve for any score that is larger for the positive class | `roc_auc_score(y == 1, spe)` | Ch. 9 |

| `permutation_importance(model, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=10)` (`sklearn.inspection`) | drop of the score when one feature is shuffled; mean in `.importances_mean` | see Chapter 8 | Ch. 8 |
| `PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator(model, X, [feature])` (`sklearn.inspection`) | partial dependence plot: average prediction along one feature | see Chapter 8 | Ch. 8 |

### Unsupervised learning

| Function | What it does | Example | Used in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `PCA(k)` (`sklearn.decomposition`) | principal component analysis with `k` components; `.transform` gives the scores, `.inverse_transform` maps them back, `.explained_variance_` and `.explained_variance_ratio_` the variance per component | `pca = PCA(5).fit(Z)` | Ch. 9 |
| `KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=0)` (`sklearn.cluster`) | k-means clustering; `.fit_predict(Z)` returns the cluster of every row | `labels = KMeans(3, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Z)` | Ch. 9 |
| `silhouette_score(Z, labels)`, `adjusted_rand_score(a, b)` (`sklearn.metrics`) | quality of a clustering; agreement of two groupings (1 = identical, 0 = random) | `silhouette_score(Z, labels)` | Ch. 9 |
| `IsolationForest(n_estimators=300, random_state=0)` (`sklearn.ensemble`) | anomaly detection; `-model.score_samples(Z)` is an anomaly score (larger = more unusual) | `score = -iso.score_samples(Z)` | Ch. 9 |

| Function | What it does | Used in |

| `sns.heatmap(table)` | coloured table, e.g. a correlation matrix or a profile hour × weekday | Ch. 1, 2 |
| `s.plot()`, `df.plot()` | quick line plot directly from pandas, e.g. of a time series | Ch. 2 |
| `s.plot.bar()` | bar chart, e.g. of the frequencies from `value_counts()` | Ch. 2 |
| `fig, axes = plt.subplots(rows, cols)` | several plots in one figure | Ch. 2 |
| `plt.show()` | displays the figure | Ch. 1 |

::: {.callout-tip}
## pandas, seaborn and Matplotlib
pandas and seaborn do not draw themselves – they call Matplotlib. These three lines produce essentially the same line plot:

```python
ax.plot(df.index, df["Appliances"], lw=0.3)        # Matplotlib
df["Appliances"].plot(ax=ax, lw=0.3)                # pandas
sns.lineplot(x=df.index, y=df["Appliances"], ax=ax) # seaborn
```

pandas takes the x-axis from the index (a time index gives a date axis) and draws one line per column, labelled with its name. Matplotlib options such as `lw`, `alpha`, `color` or `label` are passed on. With `ax=...`, pandas and seaborn draw into an existing field created by `plt.subplots`; without it, they create a new figure. Both return this field (`ax`), so you can continue with the usual Matplotlib commands, e.g. `ax.set(ylabel="...")`.

Rule of thumb: pandas for quick plots directly from a table, seaborn for statistical plots (histogram, box plot, heatmap), Matplotlib via `ax` for fine-tuning.
:::
